SITUATION OVERVIEW

• Zimbabwe is closely monitoring forecasts from the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), which indicate the potential for El Niño conditions during the 2026/2027 agricultural season. While more localised and detailed forecasts from the National Climate Outlook Forum are expected in August, the Government of Zimbabwe, supported by WFP and partners, is enhancing preparedness through anticipatory action, climate risk monitoring, early warning systems and contingency planning to safeguard food security, protect livelihoods and reduce the impact of potential climate-related shocks on vulnerable communities.

• Zimbabwe continues to face intersecting climatic and structural pressures that are driving food insecurity and livelihood stress. Recurrent climate shocks have disrupted agricultural production, increasing vulnerability in both rural and urban areas.

• Through its 2022–2026 Country Strategic Plan,

WFP Zimbabwe is delivering life‑saving food and nutrition assistance while scaling up resilience‑building efforts and strengthening early warning and social protection systems. At the same time, WFP is investing in government capacity to lead and ultimately assume full ownership of programme delivery, while partnering with the private sector to accelerate progress towards Zero Hunger.

related.title: German Military Power Needs to Go It Alone
related.summary: NATO’s European forces are already burdened by disjointed structures, national caveats, and cumbersome chains of command—and the way they have been assembled into multinational forces is a product of intra-alliance diplomacy during peacetime, not of a laser focus on effectiveness in war. Others wonder whether European NATO members are heading toward a genuinely integrated defense of their continent—or simply back to rival national armies now that the United States no longer leads.
bullets: NATO’s European forces are already burdened by disjointed structures, national caveats, and cumbersome chains of command—and the way they have been assembled into multinational forces is a product of intra-alliance diplomacy during peacetime, not of a laser focus on effectiveness in war.
Others wonder whether European NATO members are heading toward a genuinely integrated defense of their continent—or simply back to rival national armies now that the United States no longer leads.

But those who worry about a mighty Germany going it alone need to face an uncomfortable truth: NATO needs a powerful German military backed by the continent’s biggest economy and deepest fiscal pockets.
That’s because NATO’s current multinational force structures are a relic of Europe’s post-Cold War peace era.
With the United States dropping out as NATO’s integrator and technological enabler, the disadvantages of the alliance’s current structure will multiply.
related.excerpt: Old reflexes are stirring across Europe. When German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told the Bundestag last year that Germany must field the strongest conventional army in Europe and backed that promise with bigger defense budgets than any of the country’s neighbors could afford, the specter of German military power began to haunt Europe once more. Behind closed doors, some French and Polish officials ask whether a rearmed Germany really solves Europe’s dependence on the United States— or merely swaps one hegemon for another. Others wonder whether European NATO members are heading toward a genuinely integrated defense of their continent—or simply back to rival national armies now that the United States no longer leads. The reflex against a reaming Germany, however, is as much industrial as it is strategic. In June, Berlin withdrew from a Franco-German-Spanish program to build a new fighter jet—in part because Germany would no longer let a French company claim the lion’s share of the work—and scrapped a major contract with a Dutch-led consortium for naval frigates, ordering new ones from a German defense contractor instead.
